places.name: Chennai
places.summary: Tamil Nadu's capital on the Bay of Bengal: Marina Beach, Fort St George, Mylapore's temples, the Government Museum's bronzes and the classic South Indian breakfast.
places.seoTitle: Chennai Travel Guide: Fort St George, Temples & Marina
places.seoDescription: Plan your Chennai trip: Fort St George and its museum, Kapaleeswarar Temple, the Government Museum, Marina Beach, food, the monsoon and day trips.

images.alt: Aerial view of Marina Beach in Chennai with crowds and stalls along the sand
images.caption: Marina Beach, Chennai

overview.text:
Chennai, formerly Madras, grew from a fishing village that the British East India Company bought in the 17th century; it was renamed in 1996. Fort St George, dating back to 1644, was the first English fortress in India and still houses Tamil Nadu's legislature, beside a museum of colonial history.

The city is also a heartland of Tamil culture. In Mylapore, the Kapaleeswarar Temple's towering gopuram rises over the old streets, and San Thome Basilica stands over the tomb of St Thomas the Apostle. The Government Museum, founded in 1851, has a celebrated bronze gallery. Each year the Margazhi season fills the city with Carnatic music and Bharatanatyam.

Marina Beach, one of the longest urban beaches in the world, is where the city comes to stroll in the evening. Chennai is also the gateway to Mahabalipuram and Puducherry.

best_time.text: Chennai is hot most of the year: April to June is the hottest time, and most rain falls during the north-east monsoon between October and December. The weeks after the monsoon are the most comfortable, and Margazhi, the music season, brings concerts and dance across the city.

how_to_reach.text: Chennai International is India's fifth-busiest airport, with flights across India and abroad. The Chennai Metro's Blue Line runs from the airport into the city. Long-distance trains arrive at the city's main terminals; book on IRCTC.

images.alt: The colonnaded white facade of the Fort Museum building inside Fort St George, Chennai

overview.text:
Fort St George, dating back to 1644, was the first English fortress in India and the seed from which the city of Madras grew. It still houses the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly and government offices, so parts are off limits, but the historic core is open to visitors.

St Mary's Church, inside the walls, is the oldest Anglican church in India. The Fort Museum displays colonial artefacts including original letters by Robert Clive and Lord Cornwallis, and the first Indian flag hoisted after independence.

overview.text: The Kapaleeswarar Temple in Mylapore is dedicated to Shiva as Kapaleeswarar and to the goddess Karpagambal, and is believed to date back to the Pallavas. Its 37-metre gopuram towers over the surrounding streets. It is open 5:30 am–12:30 pm and 4–9:30 pm, and is busiest during its nine-day festival in the Tamil month of Panguni.

Its Bronze Gallery is the highlight, along with Buddhist sculpture from Amaravati and Pallava-era carvings; the Indo-Saracenic building also holds a rich collection of paintings by Raja Ravi Varma. places.name: Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram)
places.summary: The Pallava port town 60 km south of Chennai: Arjuna's Penance, the Pancha Rathas, cave temples and the Shore Temple — a World Heritage Site.
places.seoTitle: Mahabalipuram Guide: Shore Temple, Rathas & Arjuna's Penance
places.seoDescription: Plan a Mahabalipuram (Mamallapuram) visit: the Shore Temple, Pancha Rathas, Arjuna's Penance, cave temples, the December dance festival and the best time to go.

images.alt: The monolithic granite Pancha Rathas temples at Mahabalipuram
images.caption: The Pancha Rathas

images.alt: The giant rock relief of Arjuna's Penance carved with elephants, gods and sages
images.caption: Arjuna's Penance

overview.text:
Mamallapuram — also called Mahabalipuram — lies on the Bay of Bengal about 60 km south of Chennai. Its 7th- and 8th-century Hindu monuments, built under the Pallava kings, have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1984.

The monuments are carved straight from the granite. Arjuna's Penance is a vast open-air relief of gods, people and animals around the descent of the Ganges; the Pancha Rathas are temples cut from the living rock; and cave temples such as Mahishasuramardini hold superb panels of Durga's battle with the demon Mahishasura. Krishna's Butter Ball, a huge boulder balanced on a slope, is the favourite photo stop. Many monuments were left unfinished, so you can see how the carvers worked. On the shore stands the Shore Temple, one of the earliest structural temples in South India.

The town is also known for seafood, seashell jewellery, cafes and surfing.

best_time.text: The Ministry of Tourism recommends November to February for pleasant weather. In December, the Mamallapuram Dance Festival stages classical dance in front of Arjuna's Penance.

items.body: Start early — the monuments have little shade.
Allow a full day to see the Shore Temple, the Pancha Rathas and the hillside monuments without rushing.
Check current ASI ticket prices before you go.

places.name: Shore Temple
places.summary: The early-8th-century Pallava temple on the beach at Mamallapuram, one of South India's earliest structural temples.
places.seoTitle: Shore Temple, Mahabalipuram: History, Timings & Tips
places.seoDescription: Visit the Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram: built under the Pallava king Rajasimha, its Shiva and Vishnu shrines, the Seven Pagodas legend and opening hours.

images.alt: The pyramidal granite towers of the Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram above a green lawn
images.caption: The Shore Temple

overview.text:
The Shore Temple stands at the edge of the Bay of Bengal in Mamallapuram. It was built in the early 8th century under the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II, known as Rajasimha. Unlike the rock-cut monuments inland, it is a structural temple of granite blocks — one of the earliest in South India.

It has three shrines, to Shiva and to Vishnu, including a small shrine with Vishnu reclining. Legend tells of seven such temples, the others swallowed by the sea; the 2004 tsunami briefly exposed submerged ruins offshore, reviving the story of the 'Seven Pagodas'. Salt air has softened its carvings, but its silhouette at sunrise is unforgettable.

items.body: 6 am – 6 pm.

places.name: Puducherry
places.summary: The former capital of French India: the White Town's colonial streets, the Sri Aurobindo Ashram, Auroville and a seafront promenade.
places.seoTitle: Puducherry Travel Guide: White Town, Auroville & Beaches

images.alt: A quiet tree-lined street of colonial houses in Pondicherry's White Town
images.caption: White Town, Puducherry

overview.text:
Puducherry — Pondicherry until 2006 — was the capital of French India. It joined India in practice in 1954 and formally in 1963, but its French heritage is everywhere: in the White Town's colonial houses and street names, its bakeries and cafes, and its Franco-Tamil food. It is a small territory: in 2024 it recorded 2.12 million domestic and about 18,000 foreign tourist visits.

The town sits on the coast about 170 km south of Chennai. Its seafront Promenade Beach fills with strollers every evening. The Sri Aurobindo Ashram, founded in 1926 by Sri Aurobindo and the Mother, draws visitors from around the world, and Auroville, the experimental township they inspired, lies about 10 km to the north around its golden Matrimandir.

Franco-Tamil dishes and fresh seafood.

images.alt: Colonial houses and a parked car on a quiet street in Pondicherry's White Town
images.caption: Street in the White Town

overview.text:
The White Town, or French Quarter, is the old French residential area of Puducherry. Its cobbled streets still carry French names — Rue Dumas, Rue Romain Rolland, Rue Suffren — and are lined with yellow colonial houses, many now heritage hotels, cafes and galleries.

A heritage walk takes in the Romain Rolland Library, the French Institute, the Governor's Palace, the Church of Our Lady of Angels and the French War Memorial on Goubert Avenue, ending at the seafront promenade. The Puducherry Museum displays bronzes, coins and pottery from the region's long history.

Visit the Puducherry Museum's bronzes, coins and pottery.

places.name: Auroville
places.summary: An experimental township north of Puducherry, built around the golden Matrimandir.
places.seoTitle: Auroville and the Matrimandir: Visitor Guide
places.seoDescription: Visit Auroville near Puducherry: the experimental township, the golden Matrimandir and its silent Inner Chamber, and how visiting arrangements work.

images.alt: The golden, disc-covered sphere of the Matrimandir rising from red sandstone mounds at Auroville
images.caption: The Matrimandir, Auroville

overview.text:
Auroville is an experimental township about 10 km north of Puducherry, inspired by Sri Aurobindo and the Mother. At its centre stands the Matrimandir — a vast golden sphere that seems to rise out of the earth.

The Matrimandir is not a temple in the usual sense: its white Inner Chamber has no images, organised meditations, flowers or incense, and is meant only for silent concentration. Around it, the Matrimandir Gardens are divided into 12 named parks, such as 'Harmony' and 'Bliss'. Visits to the viewing point and to the Inner Chamber follow arrangements set by Auroville, so check the official website before you go.

items.body: Arrange your Matrimandir visit in advance through Auroville's official website.
Keep silence near the Matrimandir.
